step1_summary: Chief complaint: Burning/stinging pain when urinating for the past ~3 days.

Symptoms: Dysuria with mild suprapubic ("lower tummy") cramp-like discomfort; one episode of visible blood in urine earlier today; foul urine odor. Denies urinary frequency, urgency, flank/back pain, nausea/vomiting, fever, chills, or GI symptoms.
Past medical history: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
Medications/Allergies: No regular meds. Tried OTC bicarbonate without benefit. Allergy to clindamycin → swelling (likely angio-edema).
Family history: No known renal/urinary diseases.
Social history: 19-y-o college student (biology). Sexually active with new boyfriend (2 mo) using condoms. No smoking; social alcohol on weekends. Lives in flat with friends.

V: Urolithiasis (bladder/ureteric stone): Hematuria and dysuria can occur when a small stone irritates bladder outlet.
I: Uncomplicated bacterial cystitis (UTI): Classic cause of acute dysuria, suprapubic pain, malodorous urine, hematuria.
Pyelonephritis: Same organisms but would usually add flank pain/fever (less likely here).
Sexually transmitted urethritis/cervicitis (Chlamydia/Gonorrhea): New sexual partner, dysuria, minimal other findings.
N: Bladder neoplasm (e.g., rhabdomyosarcoma in young adults): Visible hematuria possible but very uncommon at 19.
D: Interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome: Suprapubic pain with urinary symptoms, but typically chronic, not acute.
I2: Drug-induced hemorrhagic cystitis (e.g., cyclophosphamide) – no exposure noted but fits category.
C: Congenital urinary tract abnormality (e.g., vesicoureteral reflux) predisposing to UTIs.
A: Eosinophilic/allergic cystitis – rare, usually with gross hematuria.
T: Urethral or bladder trauma (post-coital irritation): Can cause dysuria/hematuria.
E: Poorly controlled diabetes predisposing to infection – no evidence supplied.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic presentation in young sexually active female: acute onset dysuria, suprapubic discomfort, malodorous urine, micro-/macro-hematuria, absence of systemic signs suggests lower-tract infection.
New sexual partner, no prior STD screen, dysuria can be urethral inflammation; may occur even with condom use due to breakage/incorrect use.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Urolithiasis (small bladder or distal ureteric stone)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Hematuria and dysuria possible if a stone resides at bladder neck; however flank pain and colic are usually present, making it less likely.
Suprapubic pain and dysuria fit, but age is typical; onset is usually chronic (>6 wk) and not associated with hematuria or acute start.

supporting_evidence: Acute onset of dysuria over 3 days
Female, sexually active, common demographic for UTI
No vaginal discharge → favors urinary vs vaginal source
opposing_evidence: No reported frequency/urgency (common but not mandatory)
No fever or systemic symptoms (makes upper-tract disease less likely but still consistent with simple cystitis)

supporting_evidence: New sexual partner, no prior STD screen
opposing_evidence: No vaginal or urethral discharge reported
No post-coital bleeding, pelvic pain, or inter-menstrual bleeding

supporting_evidence: Dysuria can occur with distal stone irritating bladder neck
opposing_evidence: Absence of flank/loin pain or colicky pain
Less common in 19-year-old female without predisposing factors
Presence of hematuria and malodorous urine points toward infection
